title: BARRENNESS WAS PAINFUL IN SCRIPTURE—BUT IT WAS NEVER PROOF THAT GOD HAD ABANDONED YOU
paragraphs: BARRENNESS WAS PAINFUL IN SCRIPTURE—BUT IT WAS NEVER PROOF THAT GOD HAD ABANDONED YOU

Some of the women who carried the deepest ache in Scripture were not forgotten by God. And if you have ever mistaken an unanswered prayer for evidence that God has walked away from you, you need to stay with this until the end.
There is a kind of pain that becomes especially difficult to explain when everybody around you seems to be receiving the very thing you have begged God for.
You smile at their announcement.
Then cry when you get home.
You congratulate them.
Then stare at the ceiling at 2:17 in the morning wondering why heaven seems to have remembered everybody except you.
Another pregnancy.
Another birth.
Another family photograph.
Another prayer answered for somebody else.
And somewhere underneath the smile you have learned to wear is a question you may be afraid to say aloud:
“God… did You forget me?”
Maybe your barrenness is physical.
Maybe you have prayed for a child until you no longer know what words to use.
Maybe you have watched months become years.

Maybe you have experienced the grief of infertility, miscarriage, failed treatments, unanswered questions, or the unbearable awkwardness of people asking when you are going to have children as though they were asking what you planned to eat for dinner.
Or perhaps your barrenness has another name.
The marriage that never came.
The marriage that collapsed.
The ministry that never grew.
The business that died.
The reconciliation that has not happened.
The child who still has not returned to Christ.
The prayer you have prayed so many times that lately you have begun wondering whether God is tired of hearing it.
Whatever form it takes, barrenness can whisper a terrible theology into a wounded heart:
“If God loved you, this would have happened by now.”
But Scripture refuses to let that lie stand.
Because when you actually open the Bible, something astonishing happens.
You discover women whose empty wombs became places of profound anguish—but whose emptiness was never sufficient evidence that God had abandoned them.
Sarah knew barrenness.
Rebekah knew barrenness.
Rachel knew barrenness.
Hannah knew barrenness.
Elizabeth knew barrenness.
And these are not insignificant footnotes hiding in obscure corners of Scripture.
Their stories stand inside the unfolding history of redemption.
The Bible does not sanitize their pain.
It lets us hear it.
Rachel's anguish becomes almost unbearable in Genesis 30:1:
“Give me children, or else I die.”
Those words are not polished religious language.
They sound like pain.
Rachel watched Leah bear children while she remained childless, and comparison turned suffering into something even sharper. Genesis tells us that Rachel envied her sister.
That detail matters.
Because the Bible is remarkably honest about what prolonged disappointment can do inside the human heart.
Pain can become envy.
Waiting can become anger.
Silence can become suspicion.
Somebody else's blessing can suddenly feel like evidence against you.
And perhaps you know exactly what that feels like.
You love your friend.
You really do.
But when she tells you she is pregnant, something breaks inside you.
Then guilt arrives because you think a good Christian should only feel happiness.
So now you are carrying two wounds instead of one:
the grief itself…
and the shame of how grief has affected you.
Scripture does not hide Rachel's struggle.
It records it.
And yet Rachel's anguish was not proof that she had vanished from God's sight.
Genesis 30:22 eventually says something breathtaking:
“God remembered Rachel.”
The Hebrew language behind the idea of remembering is important. The verb is זָכַר — zākar — “to remember.”
But when Scripture says God “remembered” someone, it does not mean God had suffered a lapse of memory and suddenly thought, “Oh, Rachel! I forgot she existed.”
God does not misplace His children.
Biblical “remembering” often points toward God acting faithfully in accordance with His purposes and covenant.
The waiting woman had never disappeared from His sight.
And that distinction may be exactly what somebody reading this needs tonight:
God's delay is not proof of God's amnesia.
Then there is Hannah.
Few passages portray the emotional violence of infertility more honestly than 1 Samuel 1.
Peninnah had children.
Hannah did not.
And Hannah did not suffer privately in some protected corner where nobody could touch the wound.
Her rival provoked her.
Repeatedly.
Scripture says this happened “year by year.”
Think about those words.
Year.
By.
Year.
Not one difficult afternoon.
Not one disappointing month.
A recurring wound.
A repeated humiliation.
A pain that returned with the calendar.
And Hannah wept.
She could not eat.
Her heart was grieving.
Eventually she entered the presence of God carrying so much anguish that the priest Eli misunderstood what he was witnessing.
1 Samuel 1:10 says she was “in bitterness of soul” and “prayed unto the LORD, and wept sore.”
There is a Hebrew expression behind this description of Hannah's condition: מָרַת נָפֶשׁ — marat nāfesh — conveying the idea of deep bitterness or anguish of soul.
This was not mild disappointment.
Hannah was devastated.
Yet watch what Scripture does not say.
It does not say Hannah's tears proved she had no faith.
It does not say her infertility proved God hated her.
It does not say childlessness made her less valuable than Peninnah.
And it certainly does not authorize Christians today to look at an infertile woman and assume that hidden sin, weak faith, insufficient prayer, or divine rejection must explain her suffering.
That conclusion is not ours to make.
The text does say that the LORD had closed Hannah's womb, which means we should not soften Scripture merely because the statement makes modern readers uncomfortable.
God is sovereign.
But divine sovereignty and divine abandonment are not the same thing.
That distinction is enormous.
A season you cannot understand is not automatically evidence that God has rejected you.
And the biblical story makes something else clear.
Hannah was still praying.
Still going to the house of the LORD.
Still pouring out her soul.
Still bringing the wound toward God rather than pretending it did not exist.
She did not come before Him with Instagram-ready faith.
She came crying.
Her prayer was messy enough to be misunderstood.
And God was not frightened by it.
Perhaps you have been trying to sound spiritual when what you actually need to do is tell God the truth.
“Lord, I am jealous.”
“Lord, I am angry.”
“Lord, I don't understand.”
“Lord, watching them receive what I prayed for hurts.”
“Lord, I know You are good, but right now I cannot understand what You are doing.”
That is not permission to accuse God of evil.
It is permission to stop pretending before the God who already knows your heart.
Biblical faith is not emotional dishonesty.
The Psalms prove that repeatedly.
Faith can weep.
Faith can lament.
Faith can ask how long.
Faith can tremble while still reaching toward God.
Then centuries later, another woman appears in the Gospel of Luke.
Elizabeth.
Luke 1:6 gives us a detail that should permanently destroy the cruel idea that infertility automatically reveals spiritual failure.
Elizabeth and Zechariah are described as righteous before God, walking faithfully in His commandments.
And the next verse tells us:
“But they had no child, because that Elisabeth was barren, and they both were now well stricken in years.”
Do not rush past the sequence.
Faithful.
And childless.
The Greek word used for “barren” is στεῖρα — steira.
Luke does not present Elizabeth's condition as proof that she was spiritually defective.
In fact, he has just told us something about the couple's faithfulness.
That should make us extraordinarily careful about the things Christians say to suffering people.
“Maybe you haven't prayed enough.”
“Maybe you need more faith.”
“Maybe there is some secret sin.”
“Maybe you haven't claimed the promise.”
Those words can crush people.
And unless Scripture gives us grounds to diagnose someone's suffering that way, we have no authority to manufacture explanations God has not revealed.

Jesus Himself dismantles simplistic equations between suffering and personal guilt elsewhere in Scripture. In John 9, when the disciples encountered a man blind from birth and immediately wanted to know whose sin had caused the condition, Jesus refused their simplistic diagnosis.
Not every wound is a secret code revealing that somebody has been rejected by God.
Not every empty place is divine punishment.
Not every delay means denial.
And not every prayer will be answered in the precise manner we desire.
That last sentence matters.
Because there is a dangerous way to preach Sarah, Rachel, Hannah, and Elizabeth.
We can turn their stories into a formula:
“They waited and eventually had babies, so if you believe enough, you will too.”
That sounds encouraging.
But Scripture never gives us permission to make that universal promise.
The Bible records miraculous conceptions.
It does not promise every infertile believer biological children in this present life.
We must never transform a description of what God did for one person into a guarantee God has made to everyone.
Otherwise we eventually place a crushing burden on the person whose prayer remains unanswered.
They begin thinking:
“Maybe my faith wasn't strong enough.”
No.
The Gospel gives you something deeper than a formula for obtaining the life you imagined.
It gives you Christ.
And this is where the story becomes bigger than fertility.
Because every human being eventually encounters a place where life does not unfold according to the script we wrote.
Some receive children.
Some do not.
Some marry.
Some remain single.
Some experience dramatic healing.
Some faithfully endure chronic suffering.
Some prayers receive answers that leave entire families celebrating.
Other prayers leave faithful Christians holding mysteries they will not understand on this side of eternity.
Christian hope cannot therefore rest on the promise that God will always give us the particular earthly outcome we desire.
It rests on something infinitely stronger.
Jesus Christ.
The Son of God entered our broken world.
He took flesh.
He walked among sinners.
He touched the unclean.
He welcomed the rejected.
He confronted hypocrisy.
He carried sorrow.
And ultimately He walked toward a Roman cross.
There, something that looked like catastrophic defeat became the center of redemption.
The Messiah was mocked.
Stripped.
Wounded.
Crucified.
The disciples watched their hopes bleed.
Then came the tomb.
Sealed.
Silent.
Dark.
If appearances alone were trustworthy, Friday looked like abandonment.
But Sunday was coming.
The stone moved.
Christ rose.
Death did not get the final word.
Sin did not get the final word.
Shame did not get the final word.
The grave did not get the final word.
Jesus did.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel Warrior message:
Not because Jesus promises to rewrite every earthly circumstance exactly the way we request.
But because everyone who belongs to Christ is being carried toward a redemption deeper than any temporary circumstance can destroy.
Your identity is not “the barren woman.”
Your identity is not “the man whose marriage failed.”
Not “the woman nobody chose.”
Not “the couple who couldn't conceive.”
Not “the parent whose child walked away.”
Not “the Christian whose prayer still hasn't been answered.”
If you are in Christ, your deepest identity is found in Him.
Redeemed.
Forgiven.
Reconciled.
Adopted into God's family.
Loved because of Christ, not because your life resembles somebody else's testimony.
And perhaps this is where the knife reaches the deepest place.
Because sometimes what we desperately want from God slowly becomes the thing we believe we need in order to know that God loves us.
A baby.
A spouse.
Healing.
Money.
Recognition.
A restored relationship.
A breakthrough.
And without realizing it, our prayer changes from:
“God, I deeply desire this…”
to:
“God, unless You give me this, I cannot believe You are good.”
That is where disappointment can become spiritual danger.
The gift begins competing with the Giver.
And Jesus loves us too deeply to tell us that our salvation depends upon receiving every earthly gift we desperately desire.
The cross has already settled the question of whether God moved toward undeserving sinners in love.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
Look at Calvary when circumstances tempt you to ask whether God cares.
Look at the pierced hands of Christ.
You may not understand His providence.
You may not understand the timing.
You may never receive a complete explanation for some suffering in this life.
Christianity does not require us to pretend otherwise.
But the Gospel announces that God has acted decisively in Jesus Christ to save sinners.
And that means your greatest need is not finally fertility.
It is not marriage.
It is not success.
It is reconciliation with God.
Sin is the deepest barrenness of humanity.
We were not merely disappointed people needing improved circumstances.
We were sinners needing redemption.
We could not rescue ourselves.
Religion could not cleanse us.
Good works could not erase our guilt.
Then Jesus came.
The righteous One for the unrighteous.
The spotless Lamb for the guilty.
The Savior for sinners.
He carried our sins to the cross, died, was buried, and rose again.
Grace entered the scandal.
Mercy entered the failure.
Life entered the grave.
And now the invitation is not “be impressive enough for God to accept you.”
It is repent and believe the Gospel.
Come to Christ.
Bring the sin.
Bring the jealousy.
Bring the resentment.
Bring the secret anger.
Bring the sexual sin.
Bring the bitterness.
Bring the years of pretending.
Bring the disappointment you were afraid to admit.
Bring the questions.
Bring the tears.
Bring the barren places.
But come to Jesus.
Maybe you have been angry with God for years.
Tell Him the truth and repent where that pain has turned into unbelief or sin.
Maybe you have compared your life with everyone else's until gratitude has almost disappeared.
Confess it.
Maybe you have quietly hated people whose blessings reminded you of your emptiness.
Confess it.
Maybe church became unbearable because everybody else's testimony sounded like an accusation against your life.
Come back to Christ.
Not to performance.
Not to pretending.
To Christ.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, do not manufacture a polished Christian response.
Three words.
That is enough.
Or comment, “I'm still fighting,” if your faith has been bruised but you refuse to walk away from Jesus.
Someone else reading the comments may discover that they are not the only believer crying behind a smiling profile picture.
And if God has carried you through infertility, miscarriage, prolonged singleness, unanswered prayer, or another season of deep waiting, share whatever part of your testimony you can share wisely.
Not because everyone's story will end like yours.
But because somebody needs to hear how Christ sustained you when the answer had not arrived.
This is what Christian community can look like.
Not pretending.
Bearing burdens.
Weeping with those who weep.
Pointing wounded people toward Christ.
And please hear this carefully if you know someone struggling with infertility.
Do not turn their womb into a theological investigation.
Do not demand explanations.
Do not promise what God has not promised.
Do not tell them, “Your miracle is definitely coming,” as though you have access to God's hidden decree.
Do not use Hannah as a weapon.
Sit with them.
Pray with them.
Weep with them.
Remind them of what Scripture actually promises.
Christ will not abandon His people.
Nothing can separate those in Christ from the love of God revealed in Him.
There is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
God is working toward the ultimate good of conforming His people to the image of His Son.
Christ will raise His people.
Christ will return.
Christ will make all things new.
Those promises are strong enough to carry grieving Christians without inventing promises Scripture never made.
And if your own body has become the place where your grief lives, hear this too:
Your worth is not measured by your reproductive capacity.
Motherhood is beautiful.
Fatherhood is beautiful.
Children are gifts from God.
But biological parenthood is not the entrance requirement for the kingdom of heaven.
Jesus Christ Himself never married and never fathered biological children.
The apostle Paul could speak positively about singleness.
The New Testament does not construct human worth around fertility.
Our final hope is not the continuation of our biological bloodline.
Our hope is resurrection.
That changes everything.
It means Christianity can honor the longing for children without turning children into gods.
It can grieve infertility without treating infertile people as incomplete human beings.
It can pray boldly for conception while refusing to manipulate grieving couples with false guarantees.
It can celebrate miraculous answers while standing faithfully beside those whose stories unfold differently.
That is mature hope.
Hope with tears in its eyes.
Hope that refuses counterfeit certainty.
Hope anchored not in an outcome…
but in a Person.
Jesus.
Perhaps you began reading this thinking about an empty womb.
But somewhere along the way another empty place came to mind.
The prayer.
The marriage.
The child.
The diagnosis.
The dream.
The silence.
And perhaps you have interpreted that emptiness as God's verdict on you.
Look again.
An empty place is not automatically an abandoned place.
Hannah wept in an empty place.
Rachel cried from an empty place.
Elizabeth lived faithfully through an empty place.
And at the very center of Christianity stands another empty place:
an empty tomb.
The emptiness that appeared to announce the end became evidence that death had been defeated.
That does not mean every empty place in your life will become the earthly miracle you desire.
It means emptiness does not have authority to tell you who God is.
Jesus does.
The cross does.
The resurrection does.
So cry if you need to cry.
Seek appropriate medical care if infertility is part of your story.
Receive wise pastoral care.
Talk with trusted believers.
Lament honestly.
Pray boldly.
And surrender the outcome to God without pretending surrender means the desire no longer hurts.
There is no shame in saying:
“Father, I still want this.”
There is also profound faith in eventually adding:
“But Jesus, even here, You are still my Lord.”
That sentence may cost you tears.
Say it anyway.
Because Christianity was never about forcing God to become the supporting character in the life story we planned.
It is about being reconciled to God through Christ and learning to say with our whole lives:
Jesus is enough to be Lord even when I do not understand what He has permitted me to carry.
Send it privately to the couple who may be hurting quietly.
Not as pressure. Not as superstition. Not because clicking “share” earns favor with God—nothing we do purchases grace.
Share because truth is worth carrying to wounded people.
One share can place the Gospel in front of someone whose suffering you know nothing about.
There may come a night when you need these truths again.
We want it to help sustain a growing work of biblical nourishment, discipleship, spiritual sharpening, Gospel proclamation, and Christ-centered resources.
But never confuse supporting a ministry with supporting your salvation.
Your share cannot forgive you.
Your comment cannot cleanse you.
Your generosity cannot purchase God's favor.
Only Jesus saves.
Only His blood atones for sin.
Only His righteousness can make sinners right with God.
Only His resurrection gives us living hope.
That is why everything must return to Him.
If you have never truly surrendered to Jesus Christ, perhaps the deepest question raised by this article is not whether God will give you the thing you have been asking for.
It is whether you belong to Christ.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Stop hiding behind religion.
Stop bargaining.
Stop waiting until you become “good enough.”
You will never clean yourself enough to make the cross unnecessary.
Come to Jesus because the cross is necessary.
Come because grace is real.
Come because sinners can be forgiven.
Come because shame does not have to write your final chapter.
Come because the Savior who died for sinners rose from the grave.
Let the comments become more than engagement.
Let them become testimony.
Let somebody scrolling through darkness discover hundreds of human beings saying, in different ways:
“I hurt too.”
“I waited too.”
“I questioned too.”
“But Jesus met me there.”
Because maybe the sentence you need to carry away from this entire article is not complicated at all.

The place where nothing seems to be growing may still be a place where God has never stopped seeing you—and even when He does not give the ending you asked for, the scars of Jesus forbid us from calling His redeeming love indifferent.
